guide.title: Swift to Java Conversion Guide
guide.description: Practical, deterministic mappings for converting Swift code and Swift habits into idiomatic Java 21.

categories.title: Mindset shifts
categories.summary: The big conceptual differences: memory, null-safety, value types, defaults.

categories.title: Data types
categories.summary: Primitives, overflow, boxing, optionals, tuples, enums and structs.

categories.title: String handling
categories.summary: Equality, interpolation, text blocks, UTF-16 length, method mapping.

categories.title: Lambdas and closures
categories.summary: Lambda syntax, capture rules, functional interfaces, method references.

categories.title: Control flow
categories.summary: if/guard, pattern matching, switch, loops, defer.

categories.title: Objects and initialization
categories.summary: Classes, properties, lifecycle, statics, constructors, concurrency basics.

categories.title: Encapsulation and inheritance
categories.summary: Access modifiers, scope, inheritance, interfaces, extensions, generics.

categories.title: Exception handling
categories.summary: Checked vs unchecked, throwing, catching, try?/try!, resources.

categories.title: Arrays and collections
categories.summary: Reference semantics, collection types, immutability, common operations.

categories.title: Functions
categories.summary: Static methods, labels, overloading, varargs, inout, generics.

categories.title: Unit tests
categories.summary: XCTest / Swift Testing to JUnit Jupiter.

mappings.title: ARC → garbage collector
mappings.summary: Java uses a tracing garbage collector, so reference cycles do not leak and there is no weak/unowned bookkeeping.
mappings.javaExample: private Delegate delegate;   // plain reference; cycles are collected by the GC
gotchas: There is no deinit; use AutoCloseable + try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup.
java.lang.ref.WeakReference exists but is for caches, not for breaking delegate cycles.

mappings.title: Classes are open by default
mappings.swift: final class (closed by default for public)
mappings.summary: Java classes and methods can be subclassed/overridden unless marked final, the opposite of Swift's public default.
mappings.javaExample: public final class Money { }   // add final deliberately
gotchas: Mark classes not designed for inheritance as final.
let → final is also opt-in: Java locals and fields are mutable unless you write final.

mappings.title: let / var → final / var
mappings.summary: Swift let maps to final; Java's var keyword is only type inference and works only for local variables.
mappings.javaExample:
final var count = 42;   // or: final int count = 42;
var total = 0;          // int
gotchas: Java var is NOT mutability: it means 'infer the type'. Use final for immutability.
var works only for local variables, never for fields, parameters or return types.

mappings.title: Int → long (or int)
mappings.summary: Swift Int is 64-bit on modern platforms; Java int is 32-bit. Pick int or long deliberately based on value range.
mappings.javaExample: final long count = 42L;   // or int, if the range allows
gotchas: Int32 → int, Int16 → short, Int8 → byte (byte is signed: -128…127).
long literals need an L suffix when they exceed int range: 3_000_000_000L.

mappings.title: UInt types → no unsigned types
mappings.summary: Java has no unsigned integer types; use a wider type or helpers like Integer.toUnsignedString and Byte.toUnsignedInt.
mappings.javaExample:
int flags = 0xFF;                       // widen
int unsigned = Byte.toUnsignedInt(b);   // read a byte as 0…255
gotchas: byte b = (byte) 0xFF is -1, not 255.

mappings.title: Float → float (needs f suffix)
mappings.summary: Double maps to double. Float maps to float, and float literals need an f suffix.
mappings.javaExample: final float ratio = 1.5f;
gotchas: 1.5 without f is a double literal and will not compile into a float variable.

mappings.title: Character → char (UTF-16 code unit)
mappings.java: char (UTF-16 code unit) / int code point
mappings.summary: A Java char is a single UTF-16 code unit, not a user-perceived character. Emoji and many symbols need two chars.
mappings.javaExample:
String c = "👍";          // a char cannot hold it
int cp = c.codePointAt(0);
gotchas: Use code points (String.codePoints()) when you need real characters.

mappings.title: Overflow traps → overflow silently wraps
mappings.summary: Swift traps on integer overflow. Java silently wraps around, so use Math.*Exact where overflow would be a bug.
mappings.swiftExample:
let x = Int32.max
let y = x + 1   // traps
gotchas: Math.addExact, subtractExact, multiplyExact, toIntExact all throw on overflow.

mappings.title: Generics need boxed types (Integer, Long…)
mappings.summary: Collections and generics can't hold primitives, so Java auto-boxes int → Integer etc. Boxed values compare by reference with == and NPE when unboxing null.
mappings.swiftExample:
let ids: [Int] = [1000]
let a: Int? = nil
gotchas: Always compare wrappers with equals() or Objects.equals().
List<int> is not allowed; write List<Integer>.

mappings.title: Optional type T? → nullable reference
mappings.java: String (may be null) / Optional<String> as return type
mappings.summary: Any Java reference may be null; the type system won't help. Decide an explicit null strategy for every Swift optional.
mappings.javaExample: String name = null;   // nothing in the type says this can be null
gotchas: Non-optional Swift values have no Java guarantee either: fields default to null.
Convention: Optional<T> mainly as a return type, not for fields or parameters.

mappings.title: if let / guard let → null check
mappings.swift: if let x { } / guard let x else { return }
mappings.summary: Optional binding becomes an explicit null check; guard let becomes an early return.
mappings.swiftExample:
guard let user = user else { return }
if let name { print(name) }
gotchas: `if let x = x` shadows; in Java just reuse the variable — redeclaring a local is a compile error.
For Optional<T> values: x.ifPresent(v -> …).

mappings.title: ?? → requireNonNullElse / orElse
mappings.summary: Nil-coalescing becomes a ternary, Objects.requireNonNullElse, or Optional.orElse / orElseGet.
mappings.javaExample:
String display = Objects.requireNonNullElse(name, "Unknown");
// Optional: findUser(id).map(User::name).orElse("Unknown");
gotchas: orElse(expr) always evaluates expr; use orElseGet(() -> expr) for expensive fallbacks.

mappings.title: Optional chaining x?.y → null checks / Optional.map
mappings.summary: There is no ?. operator. Use explicit null checks or chain Optional.map.
mappings.javaExample:
String city = Optional.ofNullable(user)
        .map(User::address)
        .map(Address::city)
        .orElse(null);
gotchas: Calling a method on null throws NullPointerException; nothing short-circuits automatically.

mappings.title: Force unwrap x! → orElseThrow / requireNonNull
mappings.summary: Force unwrap becomes orElseThrow() on Optional, or Objects.requireNonNull for plain references.
mappings.javaExample:
User user = findUser(id).orElseThrow();
User u2 = Objects.requireNonNull(maybeUser, "user");
gotchas: Dereferencing null already throws NPE, but requireNonNull fails earlier with a clearer message.

mappings.title: Function returning T? → Optional<T>
mappings.summary: By convention Java uses Optional<T> mainly for return values that may be absent.
gotchas: x?.foo → x.map(X::foo); x ?? y → x.orElse(y); x! → x.orElseThrow(); x == nil → x.isEmpty().
Never return null from a method declared to return Optional.

mappings.title: Tuples → record
mappings.summary: Java has no tuples. Declare a small record for multiple return values.
mappings.javaExample:
record MinMax(int min, int max) {}
MinMax minMax() { ... }
gotchas: Map.entry(k, v) is a common stand-in for ad-hoc pairs.

mappings.title: enum → enum (with fields and methods)
mappings.summary: Simple enums map directly; Java enum constants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE and can carry fields, constructors and methods.
gotchas: Raw values become constructor arguments + a field.
Enums with associated values need a sealed interface instead.

mappings.title: Enum with associated values → sealed interface + records
mappings.java: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect {}
mappings.summary: Each case with associated values becomes a record implementing a sealed interface; switch over it exhaustively.
gotchas: Pattern-matching switch (Java 21) is exhaustive over sealed types, so no default branch is needed.

mappings.title: struct → record (reference type!)
mappings.swift: struct Point { let x: Int; let y: Int }
mappings.summary: Structs usually become records: immutable, with generated equals/hashCode/toString. Records are still references; value semantics come from immutability, not copying.
mappings.swiftExample:
struct Point { let x: Int; let y: Int }
var b = a; b.x = 5   // a unchanged
gotchas: Mutable structs have no Java equivalent: copy explicitly or make the type immutable.
Record accessors have no get prefix: point.x().
Validate in a compact constructor: record Range(int lo, int hi) { Range { if (lo > hi) throw … } }

mappings.title: String/object equality: == → .equals()
mappings.summary: In Java, == compares references for objects (including String and Integer). Use equals() for value equality. This is the #1 bug for Swift developers.
gotchas: == is fine for primitives (int, double, boolean) and enum constants.
Arrays: a.equals(b) also compares references; use Arrays.equals.

mappings.title: String interpolation → formatted() / concatenation
mappings.summary: Java has no stable string interpolation (the string templates preview was withdrawn). Use concatenation, String.format or .formatted().
mappings.swiftExample: let msg = "Hello \(name), you are \(age) years old"
mappings.javaExample:
String msg = "Hello " + name + ", you are " + age + " years old";
String msg2 = "Hello %s, you are %d years old".formatted(name, age);
gotchas: Specifiers: %s string, %d integer, %.2f 2 decimals, %n newline, %x hex, %,d grouping.

mappings.title: Multi-line string → text block
mappings.summary: Text blocks work like Swift multi-line strings; the closing delimiter position sets stripped indentation.
gotchas: No interpolation inside text blocks; combine with .formatted().

mappings.title: Repeated += / joined → StringBuilder / String.join
mappings.summary: Strings are immutable. Use String.join or Collectors.joining; use StringBuilder for loops of appends.

mappings.title: count / String.Index → length() / charAt (UTF-16)
mappings.summary: Swift counts grapheme clusters; Java length() counts UTF-16 code units. Java allows direct integer indexing.
mappings.swiftExample:
let first = s[s.startIndex]   // String.Index, not Int
"👍".count                   // 1
mappings.javaExample:
"👍".length();               // 2 (surrogate pair)
"👍".codePointCount(0, 2);   // 1
s.charAt(0);                 // direct integer indexing
gotchas: Iterate real characters with s.codePoints().

mappings.title: String method mapping
mappings.summary: Most String methods have direct Java counterparts with different names.
mappings.javaExample: s.toUpperCase(); s.startsWith("a"); s.strip();
gotchas: count → length(); isEmpty → isEmpty() (isBlank() for whitespace-only)
lowercased() → toLowerCase(); hasSuffix → endsWith
replacingOccurrences(of:with:) → replace(a, b) (replaceAll takes a regex)
String(repeating: "-", count: 3) → "-".repeat(3)
reversed() → new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()
String(42) → String.valueOf(42)

mappings.title: split / components(separatedBy:) → split (regex!)
mappings.summary: Java's String.split takes a regular expression and drops trailing empty strings by default.
mappings.javaExample:
String[] parts = version.split("\\.");    // '.' must be escaped
String[] all = csv.split(",", -1);       // -1 keeps trailing empties
gotchas: split(".") splits on every character and returns an empty array.
Pattern.quote(sep) escapes an arbitrary literal separator.

mappings.title: Int("42") → Integer.parseInt (throws)
mappings.summary: Parsing returns an optional in Swift but throws an unchecked NumberFormatException in Java.
gotchas: Long.parseLong, Double.parseDouble behave the same.
Integer.parseInt(null) also throws NumberFormatException.

mappings.title: Closure syntax → lambda syntax
mappings.swift: { (a: Int, b: Int) -> Int in a + b }
mappings.summary: Lambdas use (params) -> body. Types are inferred from the target functional interface; block bodies need explicit return.
mappings.swiftExample:
{ (a: Int, b: Int) -> Int in a + b }
{ a, b in a + b }
gotchas: The lambda always goes inside the parentheses: no trailing closures.

mappings.title: $0, $1 → named parameters
mappings.summary: There is no $0 shorthand; every lambda parameter must be named. Unused parameters can be _ in Java 22+.
mappings.javaExample:
items.stream().map(x -> x * 2).toList();
map.forEach((_, value) -> System.out.println(value));   // Java 22+
gotchas: For `{ $0.name }`, prefer a method reference: Person::name.

mappings.title: Mutating captured variables → effectively final only
mappings.summary: Java lambdas can only capture local variables that are final or effectively final. Fields can still be mutated.
gotchas: this.field++ inside a lambda is allowed; only locals are restricted.

mappings.title: [weak self] capture lists → not needed
mappings.summary: this in a lambda is the enclosing instance. Cycles don't leak under GC, so capture lists have no equivalent.
mappings.javaExample: api.load(data -> show(data));

mappings.title: @escaping / trailing closures → lambda inside parentheses
mappings.summary: Every Java lambda may escape, and there's no trailing-closure syntax.
mappings.javaExample: animate(0.3, () -> view.setAlpha(0));

mappings.title: Function types → functional interfaces
mappings.summary: Java has no function types. A lambda implements a functional interface and you call its method (apply, accept, test, get, run).
mappings.javaExample:
Function<Integer, Integer> square = x -> x * x;
square.apply(4);    // square(4) won't compile
gotchas: () -> Void → Runnable.run()
() -> T → Supplier<T>.get()
(T) -> Void → Consumer<T>.accept(t)
(T, U) -> Void → BiConsumer<T, U>.accept(t, u)
(T) -> R → Function<T, R>.apply(t)
(T, U) -> R → BiFunction<T, U, R>.apply(t, u)
(T) -> Bool → Predicate<T>.test(t)
(T) -> T → UnaryOperator<T>
(T, T) -> T → BinaryOperator<T>
(T, T) -> Bool (sort) → Comparator<T>.compare(a, b) returns int
() throws -> T → Callable<T>.call()
Primitive variants avoid boxing: IntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntPredicate, IntUnaryOperator…
3+ parameters or checked exceptions → declare your own @FunctionalInterface.

mappings.title: Optional closure property → Consumer field + null check
mappings.summary: Store callbacks as functional-interface fields and null-check before calling.

mappings.title: Key paths / { $0.name } → method references
mappings.summary: Method references are shorthand for lambdas that only call an existing method.
mappings.javaExample: List<String> names = people.stream().map(Person::name).toList();
gotchas: Static: Integer::parseInt
Bound instance: System.out::println
Instance of the parameter: String::toUpperCase
Constructor: ArrayList::new

mappings.title: Returning and composing functions
mappings.summary: Return lambdas from methods and compose them with andThen / compose / and / negate.
mappings.swiftExample: func multiplier(_ factor: Int) -> (Int) -> Int { { $0 * factor } }
gotchas: A lambda cannot be generic itself; use a generic method.
A lambda can't easily call itself recursively; use a method.

mappings.title: Anonymous classes (legacy code)
mappings.summary: Older Java code uses anonymous classes where you'd now write a lambda. Inside an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object.

mappings.title: if → if (parentheses required)
mappings.summary: Conditions need parentheses and must be boolean. Braces are optional but strongly recommended.
mappings.swiftExample: if score > 90 { grade = "A" } else if score > 80 { grade = "B" }
gotchas: Ternary is identical: isOn ? "On" : "Off".

mappings.title: guard … else → inverted if + early return
mappings.summary: guard becomes an if with the inverted condition and an early exit.

mappings.title: as? / is → instanceof pattern matching
mappings.swift: if let c = shape as? Circle { }
mappings.summary: Type-check-and-bind uses pattern matching for instanceof.
mappings.swiftExample: if let c = shape as? Circle { print(c.radius) }
gotchas: as! → a plain cast (Circle) shape, which throws ClassCastException on failure.

mappings.title: switch → arrow-form switch (no fallthrough)
mappings.summary: Use the arrow form. The old colon form falls through unless you break.
gotchas: case X: (colon) silently falls into the next case without break.
Switch over enums: write the bare constant name (SATURDAY), not Day.SATURDAY.

mappings.title: let x = switch → switch expression with yield
mappings.summary: Switch can be an expression. Use yield to return a value from a block branch.

mappings.title: switch on associated values → record patterns + when
mappings.java: case Circle c -> … / case Rect r when …
mappings.summary: Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type is exhaustive; when is Swift's where; records can be deconstructed.

mappings.title: for i in 0..<n → classic for / IntStream.range
mappings.summary: Ranges become index loops, or IntStream.range (exclusive) / rangeClosed (inclusive).
mappings.swiftExample:
for i in 0..<n { }
for i in 0...n { }

mappings.title: stride(from:to:by:) → for with step
mappings.swift: for i in stride(from: 10, to: 0, by: -2)
mappings.summary: Strides become classic for loops with a custom step.
mappings.swiftExample: for i in stride(from: 10, to: 0, by: -2) { }

mappings.title: enumerated() → index loop
mappings.summary: There's no enumerated(); loop over indices.

mappings.title: for (k, v) in dict → entrySet()
mappings.summary: Iterate a Map's entries, or use map.forEach((k, v) -> …).
mappings.swiftExample: for (name, age) in ages { print(name, age) }
gotchas: HashMap iteration order is unspecified (like Swift Dictionary). LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order.

mappings.title: repeat { } while → do { } while ();
mappings.summary: repeat-while is do-while, with a trailing semicolon.
mappings.javaExample: do { attempt++; } while (attempt < 3);

mappings.title: defer → finally / try-with-resources
mappings.summary: defer becomes a finally block; for resources prefer try-with-resources.

mappings.title: class → class (one public class per file)
mappings.summary: Constructors are named after the class, new is required, and a public top-level class must live in a file of the same name.
gotchas: Avoid calling overridable methods from constructors: subclass fields aren't set yet (no two-phase init).
Fields default to 0/false/null; Swift would have forced initialization.

mappings.title: Properties → private fields + getters/setters
mappings.swift: var name: String / var area: Double { w * h } / didSet
mappings.summary: Java has no properties. Use private fields with getters/setters; computed properties become methods; didSet logic goes in the setter.
gotchas: Records use accessors without get: point.x().

mappings.title: deinit → AutoCloseable + try-with-resources
mappings.summary: There is no deinit and GC timing is unspecified. finalize() is deprecated. Implement AutoCloseable for deterministic cleanup.
gotchas: Never rely on GC to release files, sockets or locks.

mappings.title: static let/func → static final / static; no class func
mappings.summary: Constants are static final in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Statics are never polymorphic: there's no class func equivalent.
mappings.swiftExample:
static let maxUsers = 100
static func create() -> Config
gotchas: class func (overridable static) → instance method or a strategy object.

mappings.title: actors / locks / queues → volatile, synchronized, atomics
mappings.summary: volatile gives visibility (good for flags), not atomicity. Use Atomic* types or synchronized for compound operations.
mappings.swiftExample: actor Counter { var value = 0; func increment() { value += 1 } }
mappings.javaExample:
private volatile boolean running = true;           // visibility only
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();
count.incrementAndGet();                           // atomic
public synchronized void transfer(...) { ... }      // critical section
gotchas: count++ on a volatile field is still a race.
async/await has no direct Java syntax; use CompletableFuture or (Java 21) virtual threads with plain blocking code.

mappings.title: Fields get default values (null!)
mappings.summary: Java fields are silently default-initialized; local variables are not and must be assigned before use.
mappings.swiftExample: class Example { var name: String }   // compile error without init
gotchas: Make fields final to force initialization in every constructor.

mappings.title: convenience init → this(…)
mappings.summary: Constructor chaining uses this(…) or super(…), which must be the first statement.
mappings.swiftExample:
init(name: String, age: Int) { … }
convenience init(name: String) { self.init(name: name, age: 0) }
mappings.javaExample:
Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; }
Person(String name) { this(name, 0); }
gotchas: Initialization order: static initializers (once) → super(...) → field initializers/instance blocks in source order → rest of constructor.

mappings.title: Default parameter values → overloads or builder
mappings.summary: Java has no default parameter values. Use overloads that delegate, or a builder / parameter record for many options.
mappings.swiftExample: init(host: String, port: Int = 80, secure: Bool = false)

mappings.title: init? → static factory returning Optional
mappings.summary: Constructors can't return null. Use a static factory returning Optional, or throw IllegalArgumentException.
mappings.swiftExample: init?(raw: String) { guard raw.contains("@") else { return nil } … }

mappings.title: lazy var → manual lazy initialization
mappings.summary: Implement laziness in the getter. The simple version isn't thread-safe; for a lazy static singleton use the holder-class idiom.

mappings.title: Access control → public / protected / package-private / private
mappings.summary: Swift internal ≈ Java package-private (no keyword). fileprivate has no equivalent. Java adds protected (package + subclasses).
gotchas: Swift public (not open) → public + final.

mappings.title: Shadowing locals → compile error in Java
mappings.swift: if let x = x / nested let x
mappings.java: reuse the variable or pick a new name
mappings.summary: Java forbids redeclaring a local variable in a nested block (a local may still shadow a field).
mappings.javaExample:
if (user != null) { … }      // just use user
int x = 1; if (true) { int x = 2; }   // compile error

mappings.title: class Dog: Animal → extends + @Override
mappings.swift: class Dog: Animal { override func speak() }
mappings.java: class Dog extends Animal { @Override public String speak() }
mappings.summary: Use extends, call the parent constructor with super(...), and always annotate overrides with @Override.
gotchas: Every class extends Object (equals, hashCode, toString).

mappings.title: Equatable / Hashable → equals() + hashCode()
mappings.java: override equals and hashCode (or use a record)
mappings.summary: Map keys, sets, contains and indexOf use equals/hashCode. Records generate both; for classes implement them together.
mappings.swiftExample: struct User: Hashable { let id: String }
gotchas: Overriding equals without hashCode silently breaks HashMap/HashSet.
Comparable → implements Comparable<T> with compareTo returning int.

mappings.title: protocol → interface (default methods)
mappings.summary: Protocols become interfaces; protocol-extension implementations become default methods. A class can implement many interfaces.
mappings.swiftExample:
protocol Drawable { func draw() }
extension Drawable { func describe() -> String { "drawable" } }
gotchas: No retroactive conformance: you can't make an existing class implement your interface.

mappings.title: extension → static utility class (no extension methods)
mappings.summary: You can't add methods to existing classes. Use a final utility class with a private constructor, or default methods on your own interfaces.
gotchas: Extensions used for protocol conformance → put implements on the class itself.

mappings.title: associatedtype → interface type parameter
mappings.summary: Associated types become generic type parameters on the interface.
mappings.swiftExample: protocol Container { associatedtype Item; func get() -> Item }
mappings.javaExample: interface Container<T> { T get(); }

mappings.title: fatalError() stubs → abstract class
mappings.swift: func area() -> Double { fatalError("subclass must override") }
mappings.summary: Java has abstract classes. Use them for shared state/constructor logic; use interfaces for pure contracts.
mappings.swiftExample: class Shape { func area() -> Double { fatalError("override") } }
gotchas: fatalError elsewhere → throw new IllegalStateException(...) or UnsupportedOperationException.

mappings.title: Closed set of types → sealed interface
mappings.java: sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure {}
mappings.summary: sealed restricts implementors, which enables exhaustive switch.
gotchas: Swift's Result<T, E> is often just a return value + exception in Java.

mappings.title: Generics are erased at runtime
mappings.summary: Java generics are erased: new T(), T.class and instanceof List<String> aren't possible.
mappings.swiftExample: func make<T: Decodable>(_ type: T.Type) -> T
mappings.javaExample:
<T> T make(Class<T> type) { ... }
<T> T make(Supplier<T> factory) { return factory.get(); }

mappings.title: throws → checked or unchecked (decide!)
mappings.summary: Checked exceptions (extend Exception) must be declared or caught; unchecked (extend RuntimeException) need not be. Choose deliberately.
gotchas: Checked: recoverable conditions (I/O, parsing input). Unchecked: programming errors.
Never catch Error (OutOfMemoryError etc.).
Built-ins: IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, UnsupportedOperationException, IndexOutOfBoundsException.

mappings.title: enum …: Error → exception class
mappings.summary: Errors are classes extending Exception or RuntimeException; enum cases become subclasses or a message/field.
gotchas: Wrap with a cause to keep the chain: throw new RepositoryException("msg", e);

mappings.title: do { try } catch → try { } catch (Type e)
mappings.summary: No try keyword per call. Catch the most specific types first; multi-catch with |; finally always runs.
gotchas: Catching Exception broadly is usually a smell.

mappings.title: try? → catch and return Optional.empty()
mappings.summary: There's no try?; catch the exception and fall back to null or Optional.empty().

mappings.title: try! → wrap as unchecked exception
mappings.summary: try! becomes catching the checked exception and rethrowing it unchecked.

mappings.title: Resource cleanup → try-with-resources
mappings.summary: Resources declared in try ( … ) are closed automatically in reverse order, even on exceptions.
mappings.swiftExample:
let reader = try FileHandle(forReadingFrom: url)
defer { try? reader.close() }

mappings.title: Throwing closures → standard interfaces can't throw checked exceptions
mappings.java: wrap inside the lambda, or a custom @FunctionalInterface
mappings.summary: Function, Consumer etc. can't throw checked exceptions. Catch and wrap inside the lambda, or declare your own interface.

mappings.title: Array / Dictionary / Set → List / Map / Set (references!)
mappings.summary: Swift collections are value types that copy on assignment. Java collections are references: assigning shares the same object.
mappings.swiftExample:
var a = ["x"]
var b = a
b.append("y")   // a is still ["x"]
gotchas: Declare with the interface type: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Map ordering: HashMap (none), LinkedHashMap (insertion), TreeMap (sorted).
Deque/stack/queue → ArrayDeque.
Generics take reference types only: List<Integer>, never List<int>.

mappings.title: Fixed-size arrays (rare)
mappings.summary: Java arrays are fixed-size; .length is a field. Prefer List in most code.
gotchas: String[] names = new String[3] is [null, null, null].

mappings.title: let array → List.of (fails at runtime)
mappings.summary: List.of / Map.of / Set.of create unmodifiable collections, but modification fails at runtime (UnsupportedOperationException), not compile time.
gotchas: List.of/Map.of/Set.of reject null elements.
stream.toList() also returns an unmodifiable list.

mappings.title: Array methods → List methods
mappings.java: add, add(i, x), remove(i), getFirst(), indexOf
mappings.summary: Most array operations map directly, with a few traps: getFirst throws on empty, indexOf returns -1.
mappings.swiftExample: arr.append(x); arr.insert(x, at: 0); let i = arr.firstIndex(of: x); let f = arr.first
mappings.javaExample: list.add(x); list.add(0, x); int i = list.indexOf(x); var f = list.getFirst();
gotchas: count → size(); arr[0] → get(0); arr[0] = x → set(0, x)
first/last → getFirst()/getLast() (Java 21) THROW if empty instead of returning nil
firstIndex(of:) → indexOf returns -1, not nil
List<Integer>.remove(Integer) removes by value; remove(int) by index
sort() → list.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder()); reversed() → list.reversed() (a view, Java 21)
removeAll(where:) → removeIf(...); removing inside for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException

mappings.title: Dictionary subscripts → Map methods
mappings.summary: map.get returns null when missing. Use getOrDefault, merge and remove for the common Swift subscript idioms.
gotchas: dict.keys / values → map.keySet() / map.values()
dict[key] = v → map.put(key, v)

mappings.title: union / intersection → addAll / retainAll (mutating)
mappings.summary: Java's set algebra methods mutate the receiver, so copy first.

mappings.title: map/filter chains → stream() … toList()
mappings.summary: Streams are explicit: enter with .stream(), exit with a terminal operation. They're lazy, single-use, and don't modify the source.
mappings.javaExample:
List<String> result = people.stream()
        .filter(p -> p.age() >= 18)
        .map(Person::name)
        .sorted()
        .toList();
gotchas: Don't mutate outside state from map/filter.
A plain loop is often clearer for complex logic with early exits.
parallelStream() is rarely a win; measure first.

mappings.title: compactMap → filter(nonNull) / Optional::stream
mappings.summary: compactMap becomes map + filter(Objects::nonNull), or flatMap over Optional results.

mappings.title: reduce → reduce / mapToInt().sum()
mappings.summary: Use primitive streams (mapToInt/mapToDouble) for sums and averages; they avoid boxing.
mappings.javaExample:
int total = orders.stream().mapToInt(Order::quantity).sum();
double avg = scores.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).average().orElse(0);
gotchas: count() returns long.

mappings.title: sorted { } / sorted(by:) → Comparator
mappings.summary: Build comparators with Comparator.comparing and thenComparing instead of a less-than closure.
mappings.swiftExample:
let sorted = people.sorted { $0.age < $1.age }
let desc = nums.sorted(by: >)
gotchas: min()/max() take a comparator and return Optional.

mappings.title: first(where:) / contains(where:) / allSatisfy → findFirst / anyMatch / allMatch
mappings.summary: Searching predicates map to findFirst (returns Optional), anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch.
mappings.javaExample:
Optional<User> admin = users.stream().filter(User::isAdmin).findFirst();
boolean any = users.stream().anyMatch(User::isAdmin);
gotchas: prefix(n) → limit(n); dropFirst(n) → skip(n)

mappings.title: Dictionary(grouping:) / joined → Collectors
mappings.summary: Collectors build maps, sets and strings from streams.
gotchas: toMap throws on duplicate keys unless you pass a merge function.
partitioningBy(pred) splits into Map<Boolean, List<T>>.

mappings.title: zip → no built-in; use an index range
mappings.summary: Java streams have no zip. Iterate indices.
mappings.javaExample:
int n = Math.min(xs.size(), ys.size());
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { var x = xs.get(i); var y = ys.get(i); }

mappings.title: Top-level functions → static methods
mappings.summary: There are no free functions; put them as static methods on a final utility class. import static lets you call them unqualified.

mappings.title: Argument labels → no labels (descriptive method names)
mappings.summary: Java has no argument labels. Put the meaning in the method name, or use a parameter record/builder.
mappings.swiftExample: func move(from start: Point, to end: Point, animated: Bool = true)
mappings.javaExample:
void move(Point start, Point end, boolean animated) { ... }
void move(Point start, Point end) { move(start, end, true); }
gotchas: Overloading by return type alone is not allowed in Java.

mappings.title: Variadic Int... → int...
mappings.summary: Varargs work the same; inside the method the parameter is an array.

mappings.title: inout → doesn't exist (return the new value)
mappings.summary: Java passes everything by value; for objects the reference is copied. You can mutate the object but not reassign the caller's variable.
mappings.swiftExample:
func increment(_ x: inout Int) { x += 1 }
increment(&count)

mappings.title: Generic functions → <T> methods, constraints with extends
mappings.swift: func max<T: Comparable>(_ a: T, _ b: T) -> T
mappings.java: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b)
mappings.summary: Type parameters go before the return type; constraints use extends (for both classes and interfaces).
mappings.swiftExample: func firstOrDefault<T>(_ items: [T], _ fallback: T) -> T

mappings.title: XCTest / Swift Testing → JUnit Jupiter
mappings.summary: JUnit Jupiter is the standard. Any class can hold @Test methods; they don't need to be public or prefixed with test.
gotchas: setUp/tearDown → @BeforeEach/@AfterEach; class setUp → static @BeforeAll/@AfterAll
XCTAssertNil → assertNull; XCTAssertTrue → assertTrue
XCTAssertThrowsError / #expect(throws:) → assertThrows(Type.class, () -> …)
@Test(arguments:) → @ParameterizedTest + @ValueSource/@CsvSource/@MethodSource
XCTSkip / .disabled → @Disabled / assumeTrue(...)
Tests live in src/test/java mirroring the main package.
Companions: AssertJ (fluent assertions), Mockito (mocking).

mappings.title: assertEquals(expected, actual) — expected first
mappings.summary: JUnit puts the expected value first; swapping them produces misleading failure messages. Doubles need a delta.

checklist.text: Int → int or long? Check the value ranges.
Every optional (?) has an explicit null strategy (null check, Optional return, or non-null guarantee).
All == on strings, wrappers and objects replaced with .equals().
Structs → records (or immutable classes), and code relying on copy-on-assign now copies explicitly.
Enums with associated values → sealed interface + records.
Default parameter values → overloads or a builder.
Extensions → static utility methods or interface default methods.
Closures that mutate captured locals → restructured, or an atomic/holder used.
throws functions → checked or unchecked decision made deliberately.
Classes not intended for subclassing marked final.
equals + hashCode implemented for anything used as a map key or in a set.
Tests moved from XCTest/Swift Testing to JUnit, with assertEquals(expected, actual) order fixed.
